dmm-2012-team-01.title: Legendre's formula
dmm-2012-team-01.body:
Each multiple of $2$ contributes a factor $2$, each multiple of $4$ one more, and so on:
$$k=\lfloor30/2\rfloor+\lfloor30/4\rfloor+\lfloor30/8\rfloor+\lfloor30/16\rfloor=15+7+3+1=26.$$

**Answer: 26**

dmm-2012-team-02.title: Count by number of digits
dmm-2012-team-02.body:
$1$-digit numbers: $9\cdot1=9$. $2$-digit numbers: $90\cdot2=180$. $3$-digit numbers: $900\cdot3=2700$. $4$-digit numbers from $1000$ to $2012$: $1013\cdot4=4052$. Total: $9+180+2700+4052=6941$.

**Answer: 6941**

dmm-2012-team-03.title: Set aside one coin
dmm-2012-team-03.body:
Let TongTong flip $10$ of her coins first, comparing with Jim's $10$.

* If she has more heads than Jim ($p$), she wins whatever the last coin does; if she has fewer, she cannot win (the extra coin adds at most $1$, giving at most a tie).
* If they tie ($t$), her last coin decides: she wins with probability $\frac12$.

By symmetry between Jim and TongTong on the first $10$ coins, $p=q$ (the probability she has fewer), and $2p+t=1$. So her winning probability is $p+\frac t2=\frac{2p+t}2=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

dmm-2012-team-04.title: Chinese remainder theorem
dmm-2012-team-04.body:
Let $N$ be the number of potatoes: $N\equiv2\pmod3$, $N\equiv3\pmod4$, $N\equiv1\pmod5$. The first two say $N\equiv-1\pmod 3$ and $N\equiv-1\pmod4$, so $N\equiv-1\pmod{12}$, i.e. $N\equiv11\pmod{12}$. Together with $N\equiv1\pmod5$: $N=11+12j\equiv1+2j\pmod5$, so $j\equiv0\pmod5$ and $N\equiv11\pmod{60}$.

The values are $11,71,131,191,\dots$; the first that is at least $150$ is $191$.

**Answer: 191**

dmm-2012-team-05.title: Place the elements
dmm-2012-team-05.body:
Since $A\cap B\cap C=\emptyset$, the sets $A\cap B$, $B\cap C$, $C\cap A$ are pairwise disjoint, each of size $2$. Choose them: $\binom92\binom72\binom52$ ways ($36\cdot21\cdot10=7560$). Each of the remaining $3$ elements may lie in exactly one of $A,B,C$ or in none of them (it cannot lie in two, or the intersections would be larger): $4$ choices each, $4^3=64$.

Total: $7560\cdot64=483840$.

**Answer: 483840**

dmm-2012-team-06.title: Divisibility
dmm-2012-team-06.body:
The unpainted cubes form an $(n-2)^3$ cube, so there are $(n-2)^3>0$ of them ($n\ge3$), and $n^3-(n-2)^3$ painted ones. The condition $(n-2)^3\mid n^3-(n-2)^3$ is equivalent to $(n-2)^3\mid n^3$, which implies $n-2\mid n$ (taking cube roots of the ratio: if $(n-2)^3\mid n^3$ then $n/(n-2)$ is a rational number whose cube is an integer, hence an integer). So $n-2\mid2$ and $n-2\in\{1,2\}$, $n\in\{3,4\}$.

For $n=4$: $8$ unpainted cubes and $64-8=56$ painted, and $8\mid56$. So the largest is $4$.

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2012-team-07.title: Area of the region
dmm-2012-team-07.body:
We need $|x-\frac14|\le|y-\frac12|$. For a given $y$ let $d=|y-\frac12|\in[0,\frac12]$. The set of valid $x$ is $[\frac14-d,\frac14+d]\cap[0,1]$, of length $2d$ if $d\le\frac14$ and $\frac14+d$ if $\frac14\le d\le\frac12$. Since $d$ is distributed on $[0,\frac12]$ with density $2$,
$$P=2\left[\int_0^{1/4}2d\,\mathrm dd+\int_{1/4}^{1/2}\left(\tfrac14+d\right)\mathrm dd\right]=2\left[\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac3{32}\right]=\frac7{16}.$$

**Answer: $\frac7{16}$**

dmm-2012-team-08.title: Construct an equilateral triangle
dmm-2012-team-08.body:
Construct $E$ on the opposite side of $AC$ from $B$ such that $AEC$ is equilateral. Then $EA=AC=AB$. Also $\angle ABC=80^\circ=20^\circ+60^\circ=\angle BAC+\angle CAE=\angle DAE$, and $AD=BC$. So triangles $ABC$ and $EAD$ are congruent (SAS), giving $ED=AC=EC$ and $\angle AED=\angle BAC=20^\circ$.

Hence $\angle CED=60^\circ-20^\circ=40^\circ$ and triangle $CED$ is isosceles with $EC=ED$, so $\angle ECD=\frac{180^\circ-40^\circ}2=70^\circ$. Then $\angle DCA=\angle ECD-\angle ECA=70^\circ-60^\circ=10^\circ$, and in triangle $ADC$: $\angle ADC=180^\circ-20^\circ-10^\circ=150^\circ$.

**Answer: $150^\circ$**

dmm-2012-team-08.title: Law of sines
dmm-2012-team-08.body:
Let $AB=AC=1$, so $BC=2\sin10^\circ=AD$. In triangle $ADC$ with $x=\angle ADC$, the angle at $C$ is $160^\circ-x$, and the law of sines gives $\frac{AC}{\sin x}=\frac{AD}{\sin(160^\circ-x)}$, i.e. $\sin(160^\circ-x)=2\sin10^\circ\sin x$. For $x=150^\circ$: the left side is $\sin10^\circ$ and the right side is $2\sin10^\circ\cdot\frac12$, equal. The function $x\mapsto\sin(160^\circ-x)/\sin x$ is strictly decreasing on $(0^\circ,160^\circ)$, so $x=150^\circ$ is the only solution.

**Answer: $150^\circ$**

dmm-2012-team-10.title: Geometric series in the complex plane
dmm-2012-team-10.body:
With $z=e^{i\theta}$, the sum is the real part of the geometric series
$$\sum_{n\ge0}\left(\frac z2\right)^n=\frac1{1-\frac z2}=\frac{1-\frac{\bar z}2}{\left|1-\frac z2\right|^2}=\frac{1-\frac{\cos\theta-i\sin\theta}2}{\frac54-\cos\theta}.$$
The real part is $\dfrac{1-\frac{\cos\theta}2}{\frac54-\cos\theta}=\dfrac{4-2\cos\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}$. With $\cos\theta=\frac23$ this is $\dfrac{4-\frac43}{5-\frac83}=\dfrac{8/3}{7/3}=\frac87$.

**Answer: $\frac87$**
